title: Legal, Moral & Software Development — Depth Practice
subject: cs

questions.prompt: Under the UK Data Protection Act 2018 (incorporating GDPR), which is a valid legal basis for processing personal data?
options: The data was easy to collect
The data subject gave informed consent
The organisation really wants the data
questions.feedbackCorrect: Correct — informed consent of the data subject is one of the lawful bases for processing.
questions.feedbackWrong: Lawful bases include consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task and legitimate interests. Convenience, desire and storage method are not legal bases.

mistakes.misconception: Confuses a processing requirement (security) with a legal basis.
mistakes.correction: Secure storage is an obligation under the Act's principles, not a justification for processing in the first place.

questions.prompt: Under the Computer Misuse Act 1990, which act is itself an offence even if nothing is copied, deleted or damaged?
options: Using a computer in a public library
questions.feedbackCorrect: Correct — Section 1 makes unauthorised access itself an offence, regardless of what happens afterwards.
questions.feedbackWrong: The Act criminalises unauthorised access per se (Section 1), access with intent to commit further offences (Section 2), and unauthorised modification (Section 3). No damage is needed for Section 1.

mistakes.misconception: Believes possessing security tools is inherently criminal.
mistakes.correction: The offences turn on UNAUTHORISED access or intent — owning tools is not itself an offence under the Act.

questions.prompt: A company develops facial recognition for use in public spaces. Discuss TWO ethical or moral concerns this raises and one legal consideration the company must address in the UK.

markScheme.text: Concern: mass surveillance / erosion of privacy in public life.
Concern: algorithmic bias — recognition accuracy differing across demographic groups, leading to unfair treatment.
Alternatively or additionally: consent — people cannot meaningfully opt out of being scanned in public; function creep beyond the stated purpose.
Legal: compliance with the Data Protection Act 2018 / GDPR — facial templates are biometric personal data requiring a lawful basis and impact assessment.

questions.prompt: Which development methodology delivers working software in short repeated cycles with continuous customer feedback?
questions.feedbackCorrect: Correct — agile methods iterate in short cycles (sprints) with frequent delivery and feedback.
questions.feedbackWrong: Agile is the iterative, feedback-driven approach. Waterfall completes each phase once in sequence; the V-model pairs testing with specification stages.

mistakes.correction: Waterfall has phases but no repetition — each stage completes fully before the next begins, with no cyclic delivery.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between black-box and white-box testing, and give one situation where each is the more appropriate choice.

markScheme.text: Black-box tests behaviour against the specification without knowledge of the internal code structure.
White-box designs tests using knowledge of the code's internal logic and paths.
Black-box appropriate e.g. acceptance testing by users, or testing a third-party module whose code is unavailable.
White-box appropriate e.g. ensuring every branch of a safety-critical algorithm is exercised.

questions.prompt: A program must accept ages from 18 to 65 inclusive. Which set of test values best applies boundary (edge) analysis?
questions.feedbackCorrect: Correct — testing just inside and just outside each boundary (17/18 and 65/66) catches off-by-one errors.
questions.feedbackWrong: Boundary analysis probes both sides of each edge: the largest invalid and smallest valid values. Middle values don't exercise the comparisons that most often go wrong.

mistakes.correction: Valid-only tests can't catch a boundary that's too loose — a comparison wrongly accepting 17 or 66 would still pass. You need invalid neighbours too.

questions.prompt: Describe three features of an Integrated Development Environment (IDE) that help a programmer write and debug code.

markScheme.text: Feature + benefit: syntax highlighting / auto-completion — reduces errors and speeds up writing code.
Feature + benefit: debugger with breakpoints and step-through execution — lets the programmer inspect state as code runs.
Feature + benefit: integrated compiler/interpreter with error diagnostics — immediate feedback on errors with line references (or version control integration / refactoring tools).

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between open-source and proprietary software licences, giving one advantage of each to the organisation distributing the software.

markScheme.text: Open source: source code is published and may be modified/redistributed under the licence terms; proprietary: source is closed and use is restricted by the licence.
Open-source advantage: community contributions improve the code / wider adoption builds reputation or a support market.
Proprietary advantage: direct revenue from licence sales / protection of competitive advantage in the code.
